courses.reference: NASW/ASWB technology standards; IFSW ethical principles

modules.outcome: Choose an accessible service route with the person, based on their access, preferences, privacy and support needs.
items: A shared phone can create access and privacy barriers even when a person technically owns or borrows a device.
A referral service assumes everyone with a phone can attend a private video appointment. A person shares one phone with several relatives. What should the worker establish first?
Whether a private, affordable and accessible channel is available to that person
Whether the phone is the newest model
Whether relatives can attend every appointment
Whether video appointments are faster for staff
Phone access alone does not establish privacy or usability. Device age, staff convenience and family attendance do not resolve the person's access needs.
Test a proposed channel with people affected by access barriers before scaling it; a staff-only test misses real usage conditions.
An online intake form works well on staff laptops but residents report difficulty using it. Which pilot would best test inclusion?
Observe willing users with varied access needs completing representative tasks
Ask the software supplier to confirm that it is modern
Count how many staff members prefer the new design
Launch it everywhere and review only completed forms
A representative task-based pilot can expose barriers among people unable to complete the form. Successful submissions alone exclude those who dropped out.
An alternative route should provide a comparable opportunity to use a service, not a punitive or indefinitely delayed option.
A learner cannot afford mobile data. The service offers an offline appointment only after all online applicants have been seen. What is the main design problem?
The alternative route introduces unequal access through avoidable delay
An offline route automatically prevents confidentiality
The learner must acquire a better phone first
Digital and offline routes must use identical equipment
Comparable access concerns the opportunity and timeliness of service, not identical technology. An alternative should not disadvantage users merely for being offline.
Ask about functional access needs instead of inferring digital ability from age, disability or education.
A worker assumes an older resident cannot use a digital service. What is the best next step?
Ask the resident about preferences and support needs, then offer suitable choices
Arrange a family proxy without consulting the resident
Exclude the resident from digital options
Require the resident to demonstrate every phone function
Individual preferences and practical needs are relevant; age-based assumptions and unnecessary tests can remove choice.
Measure service completion and abandonment by route, using proportionate data and user feedback; logins alone do not demonstrate inclusion.
A digital service reports twice as many logins after redesign. Which additional information would best test whether access improved?
Completion and drop-off patterns across access routes, alongside user feedback
The colour most frequently used in the interface
The number of devices purchased for managers
The total number of emails sent by the supplier
Login volume does not show whether people obtained support. Completion, drop-off and feedback help reveal remaining barriers.

modules.outcome: Design a proportionate information-handling plan and identify when local governance advice is required.
items: Before collecting information, specify its purpose, who needs it, how it is protected and which locally approved retention rules apply.
A new appointment form requests full family histories although it only schedules a call. Which revision best fits its purpose?
Collect the contact and access details necessary to arrange the call
Retain the full history in case a future project needs it
Require extra identity documents for every enquiry
Ask relatives to submit their records as well
The task is scheduling. Unrelated histories add exposure without helping that task; additional data requires a justified purpose.
Consent discussions should explain the channel's use, foreseeable privacy limitations and available alternatives in understandable language.
A person signs a generic form but says they do not know who can read messages sent through the service. What should happen next?
Explain access and relevant risks, check understanding and revisit the communication choice
Treat the signature as proof that every risk was understood
Ask the person to find the platform's technical specification
Continue collecting sensitive details before discussing access
A signature does not resolve an expressed misunderstanding. The worker should support an informed choice before proceeding with the channel.
An approved channel must still be used appropriately: check the intended recipient and share only necessary information.
A worker is about to send a sensitive attachment through an approved system. Two contacts have the same surname. What is the safest next step?
Verify the intended recipient and the necessary contents before sending
Send it to both contacts to avoid delay
Assume the first autocomplete suggestion is correct
Move the attachment to a personal account
An approved platform does not prevent a wrong-recipient error. Recipient verification and proportionate disclosure address the immediate risk.
A suspected information incident needs prompt action through the organisation's incident route; preserve relevant facts and follow containment instructions.
A worker discovers that a case attachment went to the wrong recipient. What is the best initial response within role?
Use the incident-reporting route promptly and follow authorised containment steps
Wait until the next annual review to disclose it
Erase the activity record before anyone sees it
Ask colleagues to keep the event informal
Reporting enables assessment and containment. Concealing the event or destroying its record can obstruct an appropriate response; notification duties need local advice.
Retention periods and exceptions require applicable policy and legal review; neither indefinite retention nor immediate deletion is a universal rule.
A team asks how long all client messages must be kept. What is the appropriate basis for deciding?
The applicable retention schedule and legal requirements, verified with the responsible lead
A universal seven-day deletion rule for every service
Unlimited retention because storage is cheap
The default setting of whichever phone is used
The draft cannot prescribe a universal duration. The decision depends on the record purpose and applicable requirements.

modules.outcome: Recognise unsuitable digital practice and maintain accountable human judgement when using AI assistance.
items: Telepractice needs a suitability and privacy check plus an agreed response to connection loss or urgent concerns, adapted to the service and local procedures.
At the start of a remote appointment the worker learns the person cannot speak privately. What is the best response?
Discuss a safer suitable channel or time and apply the service's risk procedure if needed
Continue because the appointment has already started
Require the person to disclose the concern in the shared room
Record the whole household to document the barrier
The absence of privacy changes suitability. A safer arrangement should be considered without forcing disclosure or adding intrusive recording.
Check AI-generated statements against reliable case information; an AI draft is not a verified record or an accountable decision-maker.
An AI summary adds a referral that is absent from the verified notes. What should the worker do before using it?
Check the original information and correct or remove the unsupported statement
Accept it because the text sounds professionally written
Ask the person to confirm a referral without disclosing the uncertainty
Keep it because a later worker might make that referral
Plausible wording is not evidence. The worker remains responsible for the accuracy of any record they use.
Do not enter identifiable case material into an unapproved AI service; use authorised tools and information-governance procedures.
A free AI tool asks a worker to paste a named case history to improve a draft. The organisation has not approved the tool. What should the worker do?
Use an approved workflow and seek governance advice before sharing case information
Paste it because the account is password-protected
Remove only the first name and assume the rest is anonymous
Share it and ask permission afterwards
A password or partial name removal does not establish an authorised, safe disclosure. Approval and data handling must be considered first.
Review differential effects and error patterns before relying on an automated recommendation; average performance can hide exclusion.
A triage tool performs well overall but frequently misroutes requests written in a minority language. What needs review?
The unequal error pattern and safer routing options for affected users
Only the overall accuracy because it is higher than last year
Only whether staff like the dashboard
Whether affected users can be removed from the evaluation
The subgroup pattern identifies a specific access risk. An overall average can conceal it, and excluding affected users would hide the problem.
A professional should be able to explain and document the reasons for a decision, including how an AI suggestion was checked and when advice was sought.
A worker rejects an AI recommendation after finding a factual error. Which record best supports accountability?
The relevant error, verified information, final reasoning and any consultation
Only the final AI confidence score
A statement that the computer made the decision
No record because AI was not ultimately followed
A concise reasoning record explains the human decision and its basis; the score alone does not.

courses.reference: IPCC AR6 synthesis; IFSW ethical principles

modules.outcome: Distinguish a climate hazard from unequal exposure, vulnerability and capacity to respond.
items: A hazard map does not fully describe social risk: exposure, housing, livelihood dependence and capacity to respond can differ within the same area.
Two neighbourhoods face similar flood forecasts. One has accessible transport and secure housing; the other lacks both. What should a social-risk review examine?
How living conditions and response capacity change the consequences of the hazard
Only whether the forecast uses the same colour for both areas
Only which area pays more property tax
Whether all residents can be assigned an identical risk score
The same forecast can have different consequences. Social conditions and available support matter to the review.
Do not describe communities only through deficits; identify local knowledge, mutual support and resources alongside constraints.
A climate assessment lists only residents' weaknesses. What information would improve the assessment?
Residents' existing knowledge, networks and adaptation resources
A replacement list written without residents
Only the value of imported equipment
An assumption that outside organisations must make every decision
An asset-aware assessment can identify feasible locally supported actions rather than treating residents as passive recipients.
Displacement-related planning must consider access to livelihoods, services, relationships and meaningful participation; moving people is not itself proof of a just outcome.
A relocation proposal reduces flood exposure but moves families far from jobs and accessible services. What is the most useful next analysis?
The combined safety, livelihood and access effects with affected residents
Only the number of buildings constructed
Only whether the new site is outside the mapped flood zone
Whether residents can be excluded from the final discussion
A single improvement does not establish the overall effect. Trade-offs need to be understood with those affected.
Participation records should identify whose perspectives are missing, not equate attendance with representation.
A climate consultation is attended mainly by property owners, although many residents rent. What is the main evidence gap?
The experiences and priorities of renters and other absent groups
A lack of enough photographs of the meeting
A need to count property owners twice
Proof that renters have no relevant experience
Attendance by one group cannot establish the views of groups that were not reached.
Separate observed local impacts from explanations that need specialist evidence; avoid attributing every individual event to climate change without support.
A worker documents repeated heat-related disruption at a community centre. Which statement best respects the evidence available?
Describe the observed disruption and seek relevant climate evidence before making attribution claims
State that this single observation proves the cause of every local heat event
Remove the observation because the worker is not a climate scientist
Present an assumed future temperature as a measured fact
The observation is useful, but stronger causal claims need additional evidence. Recording its limits preserves credibility.

modules.outcome: Compare adaptation options with communities, including accessibility, maintenance and unintended consequences.
items: Co-design begins while choices can still change; consultation after a fixed design offers limited influence.
An adaptation project asks residents for views after the contractor and design are final. What would make the next planning cycle more participatory?
Involve residents before options are fixed and show how their input changes decisions
Invite residents only to the opening ceremony
Ask residents to endorse the existing design without changes
Publish a survey after all funds are spent
Input has greater practical value when participants can influence meaningful choices and see the response.
An adaptation option may reduce one risk while shifting burdens elsewhere; assess who benefits and who may be harmed.
A drainage project protects a commercial area but diverts water toward lower-income homes. What is the key review question?
Whether the design transfers risk and what safer alternatives are available
Whether the protected buildings look newer
Whether the project can omit the affected homes from reports
Whether the budget was spent on time
Risk reduction in one place can worsen another group's exposure. Delivery speed alone does not establish an equitable result.
Accessible services need usable routes, communication and support; a nominal facility is not enough if intended users cannot reach or use it.
A cooling centre is free but has steps at every entrance. Which change best addresses the identified access barrier?
Work with disabled residents to provide a safe usable access route and necessary support
Advertise that admission is free more often
Count everyone in the district as already served
Require residents to provide their own lifting assistance
The issue is practical access, not price alone. A usable route should be designed with the people affected.
Compare adaptation options over their operating life, including responsibility and resources for upkeep.
A donated water-storage system has no maintenance owner or budget. What should be resolved before treating it as a sustainable service?
Who maintains it, with what resources, training and reporting arrangements
Only which donor logo will appear on it
Only the installation date
Whether the purchase price can be reported as zero
Installation does not guarantee continued service. Ownership and upkeep resources are part of feasibility.
Combine appropriate technical advice with community knowledge; conflicting accounts should prompt investigation rather than automatic dismissal.
Residents report that a proposed meeting site becomes inaccessible during heavy rain, but the planning map shows no problem. What should the team do?
Investigate the discrepancy with residents and relevant technical partners
Reject the residents' account because it is not a map
Discard every technical source immediately
Proceed and collect complaints only after launch
Different evidence sources may reveal different conditions. Investigating the discrepancy can improve the plan.

modules.outcome: Assess how climate decisions distribute benefits and burdens and propose accountable follow-up.
items: A transition plan should examine who loses income or access as well as who gains; affected workers and communities need a meaningful role.
A cleaner-energy programme closes a polluting facility but offers no plan for affected workers. What should a just-transition review add?
Worker and community participation in assessing livelihood impacts and support options
Only the project's emissions estimate
A statement that all workers will automatically find new work
A rule preventing workers from raising concerns
Environmental benefits do not erase distributional consequences. Livelihood effects and participation need explicit attention.
An accountability route needs accessible reporting, a responsible responder and a way to track responses without exposing complainants unnecessarily.
Residents can submit climate-project complaints, but nobody is assigned to respond. What is the most important missing element?
A clear response owner and a trackable follow-up process
A larger complaint box with the same process
A requirement to publish every complainant's name
A limit allowing complaints only on opening day
Collecting complaints without responsibility for action does not establish an effective accountability route.
Disaggregate benefits where appropriate and safe: an average can hide who is not being reached.
A programme reports improved average access to water. Which further check best tests fairness?
Whether improvement reaches groups facing the greatest access barriers
Whether the average can be rounded upward
Whether the report contains more project photos
Whether unsuccessful households can be excluded from the denominator
A positive average may coexist with persistent exclusion. Distribution matters alongside the headline result.
Use evidence that matches the claim and acknowledge uncertainty when communicating with decision-makers.
A campaign has ten resident interviews about a local drainage issue. Which claim is best supported?
These interviews describe concerns that warrant further local investigation
The interviews prove the exact prevalence across the country
Every resident agrees with every interviewee
The project is guaranteed to solve all future flooding
The interviews provide situated accounts, not a national prevalence estimate or a guarantee.
Review an intervention when evidence shows new burdens; record the concern, consult affected people and use the authorised adjustment process.
Monitoring shows an adaptation project's fees exclude some intended users. What is the best next step?
Review affordability with affected users and responsible decision-makers, then consider adjustments
Keep the fees unchanged because the launch was successful
Stop recording low-income users
Declare the exclusion unrelated without investigation
Monitoring should inform decisions. The observed barrier calls for review rather than removal from the evidence.

courses.reference: NASW/ASWB supervision standards; IFSW ethical principles

modules.outcome: Clarify decision authority, conflicts of interest and accountability in programme teams.
items: Delegation should state the decision scope, constraints, support and escalation route; it is not unlimited transfer of responsibility.
A coordinator tells a new worker to 'handle the whole project' without defining authority. What is the first governance improvement?
Agree which decisions the worker can make and which require approval or escalation
Assume the worker can sign every contract
Remove all supervision to demonstrate trust
Judge the worker only after the project ends
Clear authority reduces ambiguity and supports appropriate decisions; vague delegation does not establish permission for every action.
When personal interests could influence a decision, disclose the conflict and use the organisation's independent decision process.
A manager is choosing a supplier owned by a close relative. What is the best next step?
Declare the conflict and follow the procurement and recusal process
Approve the supplier privately because it may be faster
Ask the relative to offer a personal reward
Omit the relationship from the decision record
Disclosure and independent handling protect the decision process. A potentially useful supplier does not remove the conflict.
Record the decision, its reasons, authority, owner and review point; minutes that only say 'agreed' do not establish accountability.
A team cannot explain why it changed a service schedule. Which record would have helped most?
The reason, authorised decision, responsible owner and review date
Only a list of attendees' favourite options
Only the total meeting duration
Only the manager's job title
A decision record connects the choice to its basis and follow-up, not merely to who was present.
Invite relevant perspectives before decisions and explain how disagreement was handled; inclusion is more than unanimous-looking minutes.
Frontline workers raise workload concerns but meeting minutes record only management's preferred option. What should the team improve?
Record and examine the concerns and explain the final decision
Delete the concerns to preserve a positive tone
Stop inviting frontline workers
Require workers to agree before they can speak
A defensible process can reach a decision despite disagreement while retaining and responding to relevant evidence.
Authority to manage a programme does not automatically confer competence or permission to perform specialist professional tasks.
A programme lead is asked to provide specialist clinical advice outside their training. What should they do?
Recognise the limit and arrange appropriate qualified support through the agreed route
Give the advice because they manage the budget
Ask a junior worker to give it under the lead's name
Use an online summary as a substitute for competence
Management responsibility does not establish specialist competence. Appropriate consultation or referral protects role boundaries.

modules.outcome: Use structured supervision to support learning, wellbeing and safe escalation.
items: A supervision agreement should clarify purpose, roles, regularity, records, confidentiality limits and routes for urgent concerns.
A supervisee believes everything said in supervision is absolutely secret. What should the supervisor clarify?
The agreement's confidentiality limits and how safety or other reportable concerns are handled
That no concern can ever leave the room
That all discussions will be posted publicly
That keeping no record removes every confidentiality issue
Supervision needs clear expectations. Neither absolute secrecy nor indiscriminate disclosure is an appropriate default.
Reflective supervision explores observations, assumptions, emotions and alternatives, then agrees a learning action; it is more than checking task counts.
A worker says, 'I assumed the family was unwilling because they missed two appointments.' Which prompt best encourages reflection?
What evidence supports that view, what alternatives are possible, and how could you check them?
How can you close the case before the end of the day?
Can you repeat the assumption in stronger language?
Which colleague can be blamed for the missed appointments?
The prompt separates evidence from interpretation and opens a practical learning step rather than reinforcing an untested judgement.
Supportive supervision does not replace urgent safeguarding or incident procedures; use the appropriate route without waiting for a scheduled session.
A worker reports an immediate safeguarding concern shortly before a routine supervision meeting next week. What should the supervisor advise?
Use the applicable urgent safeguarding route now and arrange support alongside it
Save the concern for next week's reflective discussion
Ask the worker to keep it off the record
Treat a supportive conversation as completion of all required action
Reflection and support are valuable but do not substitute for timely action through the appropriate safety procedure.
Feedback should identify specific behaviour and its effect, invite the worker's perspective, and agree a feasible improvement and review.
A supervisor wants to address incomplete handovers. Which feedback is most useful?
Discuss a specific missing handover detail, its effect and an agreed improvement
Tell the worker they are generally careless
Compare the worker's personality with a colleague's
Avoid feedback until the annual review
Specific, actionable feedback supports learning and follow-up; personal labels do not explain what should change.
Repeated overload is a work-design issue to review as well as an individual support concern; consider case demands, resources and safe priorities.
Several workers miss breaks and report growing backlogs. What is the best supervisory response?
Review workload and resources, agree safe priorities and offer support
Offer a wellbeing poster while leaving all demands unchanged
Treat every backlog as proof of poor motivation
Cancel supervision until the backlog disappears
Support should address the conditions contributing to overload, not only encourage individuals to cope.

modules.outcome: Use delivery information to manage risks, resources and authorised programme adjustments.
items: Track an implementation issue with its impact, owner, action and review date; a list without follow-up is not a management response.
A referral partner repeatedly misses agreed handovers. What should the programme lead record and act on?
The effect on service continuity, responsible contacts and a dated corrective action
Only the partner's logo
Only the original launch announcement
A note to discuss it at an unspecified future time
A clear owner and follow-up make the issue actionable and connect it to service continuity.
A variance from plan should be explained before action: compare intended and actual delivery, investigate causes and consider service effects.
A programme is spending less than planned because accessible transport has not been provided. How should the lead interpret the underspend?
As a possible delivery gap requiring investigation, not automatically as success
As proof that the service became more efficient
As permission to remove the transport budget permanently
As irrelevant because the accounts balance
Lower spending may reflect unmet service needs. Financial totals must be interpreted with delivery information.
Changes beyond delegated limits require approval; document why a change is proposed and its likely effects before committing resources.
A coordinator wants to move funds to a new activity outside their delegated authority. What should happen first?
Submit the reason and implications through the authorised change process
Commit the money and request approval at year end
Describe the new activity under the old budget label
Ask a supplier to hide the change in an invoice
The proposed change needs proper authority and a transparent record; relabelling does not create permission.
Distinguish a delivery count from a result for participants; both can be useful but they answer different questions.
A report says 200 sessions were delivered and therefore every participant's wellbeing improved. What is the problem?
The session count does not by itself establish a participant outcome
A session count can never be recorded
Delivery and outcomes must always be numerically identical
The number is too small to report without doubling it
Delivery volume describes activity. The outcome claim needs appropriate evidence beyond the count.
A learning adjustment should state the change, owner, expected effect and review criteria, while preserving safety and authorised scope.
A pilot team changes appointment reminders after feedback. What makes this an accountable learning adjustment?
Document the change and owner, check risks, and agree how and when to review its effects
Change several unrelated processes without recording them
Assume every suggestion must be implemented permanently
Remove unsuccessful participants from subsequent reporting
A bounded, documented change can be assessed and revised; unrecorded changes make learning and accountability harder.

courses.reference: IFSW ethical principles; course-specific inquiry design examples require research-methods review

modules.outcome: Frame an answerable practice question and plan meaningful, voluntary participation.
items: An answerable practice question identifies a specific issue, population or setting and a feasible inquiry; it should not assume its conclusion.
Which question is best suited to a small inquiry about missed appointments at one service?
What barriers do participating service users describe when attending appointments at this service?
Why are all people who miss appointments irresponsible?
How can this team prove its service is perfect?
What explains every missed appointment in the world?
The bounded question can be explored without presuming blame or claiming universal reach.
Meaningful participation includes influence over relevant questions and interpretation, with roles and limits agreed in advance.
Residents are invited only to approve a finished research report. What would give them more meaningful influence in the next inquiry?
Agree involvement in framing questions and interpreting findings before collection starts
Ask for more signatures on the final cover page
Invite only residents who already agree with the conclusions
Replace discussion with a photograph for the report
Early and substantive roles can influence the inquiry. End-stage endorsement alone provides limited participation.
Separate participation choices from service eligibility; make refusal possible without threatening support, and manage power differences.
A service user thinks declining an interview will jeopardise their support. What should the team address before recruitment continues?
Clarify and protect voluntary choice and separate recruitment from service decisions
Use the fear to obtain more responses
Treat receipt of support as automatic research consent
Ask the caseworker to insist on participation
The perceived dependency undermines free choice. The recruitment process must address the power relationship.
Researchers should reflect on how their role and assumptions influence questions, recruitment and interpretation; reflection does not eliminate bias.
A worker researching their own service believes its new process must be effective. What should they do with that assumption?
Record it and seek methods and perspectives that can challenge it
Exclude any account that contradicts it
Treat their job role as proof of objectivity
Rewrite questions so every answer supports the process
Making the assumption visible and allowing challenge helps manage its influence; it does not guarantee neutrality.
Agree co-researcher roles, support, compensation arrangements where applicable, access and confidentiality expectations before tasks begin.
A resident co-researcher is asked to interview neighbours without training or a role agreement. What should happen first?
Agree the role and boundaries, provide appropriate support and review privacy risks
Give them unrestricted access to all case files
Assume living locally replaces preparation
Require them to disclose neighbours' stories at a public meeting
Local experience is valuable but does not replace clear responsibilities, preparation and information safeguards.

modules.outcome: Collect proportionate information and interpret findings without overstating what the inquiry can show.
items: Choose the minimum information needed for the question and keep recruitment contacts separate from responses where feasible.
A satisfaction inquiry proposes collecting identity numbers although its question concerns appointment times. What should the team reconsider?
Whether identifiers are necessary and whether less identifying information can answer the question
Whether more identifiers would make the report look rigorous
Whether responses can be posted with full identities
Whether irrelevant identifiers guarantee truthful answers
Identity numbers do not inherently help answer a scheduling question and add avoidable information risk.
Small groups can be identifiable through combinations of details even when names are removed; review quotations and context before sharing.
A report removes names but describes the only wheelchair user in a small village by job and household details. What is the main risk?
The person may still be identifiable from the combined description
The report becomes automatically anonymous once names are removed
Confidentiality matters only for numeric data
The description cannot be sensitive because it is written in prose
Indirect details can identify someone in context. Name removal alone is not a sufficient privacy check.
Recruitment methods shape whose experiences are represented; describe missing perspectives and avoid generalising beyond the sample.
An online survey reaches only residents who follow the service's social-media page. What should the report acknowledge?
People outside that channel may have different experiences that the survey did not capture
Every resident had an equal chance to respond
The findings prove the views of all non-users
The response count removes any recruitment limitation
Channel-based recruitment can miss important groups regardless of the total response count.
Conflicting findings should be explored and reported transparently, not removed merely to make a simple story.
Interviews praise a service, but appointment records show persistent drop-out. What is the best next step?
Explore the difference in what each source measures and report relevant limitations
Delete the records because interviews are more positive
Discard the interviews because numbers always override experience
Average the statements into an unsupported single score
Different sources can describe different experiences or populations. The discrepancy may be informative.
A before-and-after change alone does not establish that a pilot caused the result; consider other explanations and design limits.
Attendance rises after a reminder pilot during the same month transport becomes free. What can the team reasonably conclude?
Attendance improved, but the pilot's separate contribution is uncertain
The reminder pilot alone caused the entire increase
Free transport could not have any influence
A before-and-after comparison proves causation in every case
Concurrent changes create alternative explanations. The observed improvement is not enough to isolate the reminder's effect.

modules.outcome: Plan a bounded, reviewable service pilot with safeguards and a useful feedback loop.
items: Before a pilot, define the scope, participants, risks, responsible people and criteria for continuing, changing or stopping.
A team wants to try a new intake process. Which preparation best supports a responsible pilot?
Set a limited scope, safeguards, decision criteria and review responsibilities
Roll it out everywhere without a review date
Remove the current route before checking alternatives
Define success only after results are known
A bounded plan supports a defensible decision and protects participants while uncertainty remains.
A pilot label does not exempt a project from research-ethics or governance review; obtain the relevant determination before data collection.
A team says ethics review cannot apply because it calls its project 'service innovation'. What should it do?
Ask the relevant governance or ethics body to determine the applicable requirements
Assume the label settles the issue
Begin collecting sensitive data while avoiding any record
Tell participants that pilots have no privacy requirements
The activity and its risks, not just its label, determine which review requirements apply.
Stop or pause criteria should lead to timely review when harms or barriers emerge; completing the pilot schedule is not the only priority.
A new booking pilot repeatedly leaves participants unable to access urgent appointments. What is the best response?
Use the agreed safety and escalation route and review whether to pause or change the pilot
Continue unchanged to obtain a larger sample
Remove those participants from the findings
Wait until the scheduled final report before raising the issue
Emerging access risks need timely action. More observations do not justify ignoring the problem.
Record adaptations and their timing so later readers know which version participants experienced.
Halfway through a pilot, staff change the reminder script. What record is needed for interpretation?
What changed, why, when and which participants experienced each version
Only the original script because that was approved first
Only the best outcome from either version
A combined result that hides the change
Version and timing information help explain results and prevent attributing every outcome to a single unchanged intervention.
Return understandable findings to participants, explain limits and decisions, and offer a feasible way to respond.
An inquiry ends with a technical report sent only to funders. What would improve accountability to participants?
Share an accessible summary, explain decisions and limitations, and provide a feedback route
Publish identifiable raw interviews to show transparency
Promise every suggestion will be adopted
Assume participants do not want to know the outcome
An accessible feedback loop respects participation without promising agreement or exposing private data.
